around.headline: Bengaluru homemaker detained after husband, 4-year-old son found dead at home
around.summary: A woman was detained after her husband and their 4-year-old son were found dead at their Bengaluru residence, allegedly smothered; police are probing an alleged affair as a possible motive. If you or someone you know is in domestic distress, Karnataka's women's helpline (181) and police helpline (100) are there to step in before things escalate.

around.headline: Karnataka FDA launches QR-code system to report bad food and drugs
around.summary: The state Food and Drug Administration has rolled out a QR-code system letting residents scan and instantly file a complaint about unsafe or unhygienic food or medicines. Worth scanning and reporting next time something looks off at a restaurant or pharmacy instead of just leaving a bad review.

around.headline: 22 trains cancelled, 3 partially cancelled in Bengaluru today
around.summary: South Western Railway has fully cancelled 22 trains and partially cancelled 3 more running through Bengaluru on August 18. Check your PNR or train status before heading to the station this morning.

around.headline: Bengaluru flagged as worst-performing metro in voter-roll revision, 46% at risk of being dropped
around.summary: Bengaluru came out worst among major cities in the ongoing Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, with up to 46% of listed voters at risk of being struck off for non-verification. Check your name on the draft rolls and complete verification before the deadline if you want to keep your vote.

around.headline: Flu outbreak shuts Clarence School in Bengaluru for two days
around.summary: Over 500 students and 21 staff at Clarence School fell ill with flu-like symptoms, forcing the school to suspend classes on Monday and Tuesday. If your child shows fever or flu symptoms, keep them home and get them checked rather than sending them in.

around.headline: India says it thwarted attacks by Pakistan-backed militants, over 200 operatives arrested
around.summary: Indian security agencies say they foiled a series of planned attacks and arrested more than 200 operatives linked to Pakistan-backed militant networks. Expect continued heightened checks and security presence at transit hubs and public gatherings nationwide in the coming weeks.

street_smart.title: You bought a mixer-grinder online; it stops working after 10 days. The seller says it's 'out of warranty' because you didn't register it within 48 hours, and refuses a refund or replacement. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: No incident in today's feeds fit the choice-based trap format (today's real Bengaluru news — a family tragedy under investigation, a flu outbreak at a school, train cancellations, and the SIR voter-roll fallout — doesn't lend itself to a 'best move' scenario). Rotating in from the evergreen list: consumer court basics, last used 2026-07-28, which is at or just past the 3-week mark. Every other evergreen topic (digital-arrest scams, UPI fraud, auto/cab overcharging, rental/tenant traps, fake job offers, OTP/social engineering, two-wheeler theft, medical emergencies, phone snatching, loan-app harassment, credit-card skimming) has run more recently within the last 3 weeks.
street_smart.situation: The 48-hour 'registration' rule isn't written anywhere in the invoice or manual you were given, and the seller's chat support keeps repeating the same line and hanging up the chat.

choices.text: Accept it as bad luck, write it off, and buy a new one elsewhere.
choices.feedback: You're giving up a claim that's legally yours. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, a seller can't invalidate your right to a working product with a made-up 'registration window' that isn't in any official terms — you just don't know that yet.

choices.text: Pay the seller's quoted 'out-of-warranty service fee' since it seems like the fastest way to get it fixed.
choices.feedback: This is exactly the trap: a fake technicality is used to shift a cost onto you that the seller should bear. Paying it confirms the tactic works and gets you nothing you weren't already owed for free.

choices.text: Keep calling customer care repeatedly and post angry reviews, hoping they respond.
choices.feedback: This might eventually shame the seller into acting, but it's slow, unpredictable, and leaves no formal record. There's a faster, structured route that actually has legal teeth.

choices.text: File a free complaint with the National Consumer Helpline (1800-11-4000 / UMANG app), and if unresolved, escalate to e-daakhil.nic.in citing the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
choices.feedback: Correct. Keep your invoice and chat transcripts as proof, file with the National Consumer Helpline first — many disputes resolve at this stage through mediation — and if not, e-daakhil lets you file a formal consumer-court case online without a lawyer or a court visit.

takeaways: A seller's internal 'registration window' or similar in-house rule can't override your rights under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for defective goods — keep your invoice as proof regardless of what they claim.
Start with the free National Consumer Helpline (1800-11-4000 or the UMANG app) — many complaints get resolved through mediation before you need to file a formal case.

For unresolved disputes, e-daakhil.nic.in lets you file a consumer-court complaint entirely online, and for e-commerce specifically, the platform is required to have a grievance officer you can escalate to directly.

quiz.question: Which blood type is known as the 'universal donor' because it's considered safe for transfusion to almost anyone in an emergency?
quiz.why: O-negative blood lacks the A, B, and Rh antigens that can trigger an immune reaction, which is why it's kept on hand for emergency transfusions when a patient's blood type is unknown.
